title: Installing R & RStudio
markdown:
## What this covers

A short, practical guide: getting a working copy of R and RStudio in place before the course's
computational work can start, on a personal machine or through Berkeley's DataHub, and confirming
that add-on packages can actually be installed. It assumes only that the reader has a computer and
a browser — nothing about R itself.

## Installing R

The course material asks for a recent R: **if your installed version is older than 4.0.0, install
the latest release instead.** One offering of the course spells out why the cutoff sits at 4.0.0
rather than being an arbitrary "newest is best": R 3.5 or 3.6 is fine for most of the course, but a
couple of topics later in the term assume language or package features that only appear from
4.0.0 on. So the version requirement is not caution for its own sake — it is there because specific
later material depends on it.

R is downloaded from CRAN, with a platform-specific installer:

  * **macOS** — install the `.pkg` build from [cran.rstudio.com/bin/macosx](https://cran.rstudio.com/bin/macosx)
    (the course has pointed students at `R-4.2.1.pkg` in its more recent offerings, and
    `R-4.1.0.pkg` in earlier ones — take whatever the current release is, since the requirement is
    "4.0.0 or later", not a specific point release).
  * **Windows** — [cran.rstudio.com/bin/windows/base](https://cran.rstudio.com/bin/windows/base/)
  * **Linux** — [cran.rstudio.com/bin/linux](https://cran.rstudio.com/bin/linux/)

## Installing RStudio

RStudio is the IDE the course is run in on top of R, and is a separate download from
[rstudio.com/ide/download/desktop](https://www.rstudio.com/ide/download/desktop). Scroll to the
"Installers for Supported Platforms" section and pick the installer for your operating system.

## Verifying that add-on packages install

R's own installer is not enough evidence that the setup works, because the course depends on
being able to pull in packages beyond base R — the actual failure mode is a permissions problem on
the library directory, not a broken R installation. The check the course uses is to install one
add-on package, `fields`, and see whether it succeeds:

1. In RStudio, go to **Tools → Install Packages**.
2. In the dialog, type `fields` (no quotes) into the **Packages** field.
3. Depending on where the **Install to Library** field points, this may prompt for an
   administrator password.

If installing to a system-wide library is not possible — no admin rights on the machine, for
instance — packages can instead go to a directory owned by the individual user:

  * In R, run `Sys.getenv()['R_LIBS_USER']`.
  * Create the directory that command reports, if it does not already exist. On a Mac this might
    be `~/Library/R/4.0/library`.

Once that directory exists, the package install can be pointed at it instead of the system
library, and no administrator password is needed.

## Windows: a further wrinkle

Windows installs of the full toolchain — R, RStudio, and the LaTeX distribution the course
material is built with — have enough extra steps that the course keeps a dedicated Windows-only
walkthrough ("Using R, RStudio, and LaTeX on Windows") rather than folding it into the general
instructions above. That document is referred to but not reproduced here — see Sources.

## Using DataHub instead of installing locally

For anyone who cannot or would rather not install R and RStudio locally, the course runs an
RStudio session through Berkeley's DataHub, which needs only a browser:

1. Log in to DataHub — the course's separate instructions on accessing the Unix command line cover
   this login step, and are likewise referred to rather than reproduced here.
2. Once logged in, click **New** in the mid-upper right, then **RStudio**.
3. Alternatively, go directly to [r.datahub.berkeley.edu](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu), which
   skips straight to the RStudio session.

DataHub gives every student the same environment regardless of what is or is not already on their
own machine, at the cost of needing a live internet connection to work.

## Sources

This chapter is a practical howto rather than a lecture, and has no slides or transcript behind
it. It is built from the course's "Installing R & RStudio" (also titled "On your laptop" in the
earliest offering) howto page, which recurs with only minor edits across four Berkeley STAT 243
offerings:

  * `berkeley-stat243/fall-2026/howtos/RandRStudioInstall.md` (used as the primary text: the most
    recent, and identical in substance to fall-2024 and fall-2025 apart from source links and the
    exact CRAN point-release named for macOS)
  * `berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/howtos/RandRStudioInstall.md`
  * `berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/howtos/RandRStudioInstall.md`
  * `berkeley-stat243/stat243-fall-2021/howtos/RandRStudioInstall.Rmd` — the outlier: different
    title ("On your laptop"), an older macOS release named (`R-4.1.0.pkg`), and the extra remark
    about R 3.5/3.6 being acceptable except for Unit 5, which is reproduced above since it explains
    *why* the 4.0.0 floor exists.

Two documents the course refers to from this page are not themselves supplied and so are not
reproduced: "Using R, RStudio, and LaTeX on Windows" (`windowsInstall.Rmd`/`windowsInstall.html`)
and "Accessing the Unix Command Line" (`accessingUnixCommandLine.html`).
